newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rights groups hail Rwanda trials, but say flawed.
newsitem.headline: Rights groups hail Rwanda trials, but say flawed.

text.p: Two human rights groups on Monday hailed the start of genocide trials in Rwanda but slammed the court hearings as superficial and flawed by a lack of defence lawyers.

The Paris-based International Federation of Human Rights Leagues (FIDH) and the New York-based Human Rights Watch/Africa said they "welcome the holding of trials in Rwanda but deplore serious irregularities".

The first genocide trials in Rwanda opened on Friday in the southeastern town of Kibungo, where two men pleaded not guilty to organising massacres. Two other men appeared in court on Monday in Kigali but their cases were immediately adjourned.

"In the genocide trials, the accused did not benefit from the assistance of a lawyer, which represents a particularly serious violation of their rights considering they risk the death penalty if found guilty," the two groups said in a statement.
Those convicted on charges of taking part in the 1994 slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis along with Hutu moderates face the death penalty after one chance of appeal.

The FIDH and Human Rights Watch dismissed Rwanda's arguments that it lacked cash for defence lawyers, saying the U.N. had given up a project to supply lawyers in 1995 after opposition from Kigali's government.
"Political opposition is a factor as strong as the lack of funds," the rights groups said.
They also deplored "the summary character" of the trial on Friday of Deo Bizimana, a former medical assistant, and Egide Gatanazi, a former local administrator, both accused of organising massacres.

The statement said the trial lasted only a few hours and the prosecutor merely summarised witnesses' charges rather than allowing the defendants to be confronted by their accusers, a right under Rwandan law.
About 90,000 Rwandans are crammed into jails since being accused of taking part in the 1994 slaughter by Hutu troops, militias and mobs.
